headlines.article_text: JPMorgan Chase experiencing 'technical issue' Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points JPMorgan Chase on Monday said a "technical issue" was making some transactions take longer than usual for customers. A spokesperson for JPMorgan said the issue was not cyber-related and that it was not systemic. CNBC's Eamon Javers reported there was no indication of bad actors involved. In this article JPM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 3:02 03:02 No indication bad actors are involved with JPMorgan Chase technical issue Closing Bell: Overtime JPMorgan Chase reported a "technical issue" that was affecting some consumer banking services Monday. The bank said a "temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" was causing some customer transactions to take longer than usual, though it said customers can still access their accounts and funds. "There is no evidence it is cyber-related," a JPMorgan spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC. "This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," the spokesperson said. "We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today." CNBC's Eamon Javers reported there was no indication of bad actors involved. Still, other major banks were listed in outage reports as transactions between Chase and other institutions appeared to get held up. Users reported errors as early as 11:30 a.m. ET. A representative for U.S. Bank said that company was "not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays." Zelle is the peer-to-peer payments system backed by many of the largest U.S. banks, including JPMorgan. The outage reports come days after separate, widespread issues with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers . — CNBC's Leslie Picker contributed to this report.
